title: Do You Have This Muscle?
sources: The palmaris longus tendon shows in the middle of the wrist when you touch the thumb to the little finger and flex the wrist (Schaeffer's test) (Thompson, Mockford & Cooper 2001, J Hand Surg Br)
Palmaris longus is absent in roughly 14% of people in European populations (about 1 in 7), varying widely by population (Thompson et al. 2001; Sebastin et al. 2005; Ioannis et al. 2015 meta-analysis)
It is considered a vestigial muscle, thought to be a remnant from primate ancestors that used it in climbing/hanging (Fowlie et al. 2012; National Geographic/UCSF summaries)
Because it is expendable, its tendon is commonly harvested as a graft for tendon and ligament reconstruction (Wehbé 1992, J Hand Surg)
Absence is often unilateral: some people have it on only one arm (Thompson et al. 2001)

lines.text: Touch your thumb to your pinky and bend your wrist. See that cord pop up?
lines.caps: Touch your *thumb | to your *pinky | and *bend your wrist | See that *cord | *pop up?

lines.text: That's a muscle called the palmaris longus.
And about one in seven people don't have it at all.
